newsitem.title: COSTA RICA: Clinton to shine spotlight on Central America.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to shine spotlight on Central America.

text.p: After riding unscathed through a potentially rocky trip to Mexico, U.S. President Bill Clinton faces more diplomatic challenges in Central America, where he will meet regional leaders at a summit on Thursday.

The Central Americans said they wanted concrete progress on a free-trade treaty with Washington and demanded better treatment for their illegal immigrants in the United States, neither topic likely to find support in the U.S. Congress.
Clinton will need to stake out a middle position between accommodating his Central American hosts but not promising anything that will be rejected back home, diplomats said.

"Yes, of course, we know these things are not popular there," Luis Guillermo Solis, director of policy in the Costa Rican Foreign Ministry, told Reuters. "But we have decided that we can't be timid as we see the world dividing up into trading blocs like Mercosur (in South America) and NAFTA (the North American Free Trade Agreement grouping the United States, Canada and Mexico)."

The tiny Central American economies, many battered by Cold War-era civil wars and lack of foreign investment, have begun integrating in recent years, forming a more formidable market of 30 million people.

After a 48-hour state visit to Mexico, Clinton is set to arrive here late on Wednesday for a meeting with the five traditional Central American countries -- Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica -- plus neighbouring Panama and Belize, and the Dominican Republic, a Caribbean island nation.

The stakes for Clinton here are not so high as in Mexico, where the explosive mix of historic conflicts, drug trafficking, a 2,000-mile (3,000-km) common border and $140 billion in annual trade have complicated U.S.-Mexican relations. Despite that, Clinton's well-orchestrated Mexico trip was decidedly upbeat.

Clinton now ventures into a territory that has a long history of clashes with the United States, which has either invaded, engineered a coup or armed a favoured side in virtually every country on the list. The notable exception is host Costa Rica, the peaceful and relatively prosperous nation in the region.
But with the Monroe Doctrine, which commits the United States to a Western Hemisphere safe from aggression, and the Cold War now history, relations have changed.
"The qualitative leap is that Central American is now talking to the United States about a free-trade treaty or access to NAFTA," Costa Rican Foreign Trade Minister Jose Manuel Salazar told Reuters.
Like Mexico, the Central Americans will seek a pledge from Clinton to do something to protect the hundreds of thousands of illegal immigrants from the region living in the United States.

The U.S. Congress passed a tough new immigration law in 1996 with many of the law's major provisions kicking in on April 1 of this year, including one that wipes out the preferential treatment on immigration matters formerly granted to Central American countries.

Nicaragua, for example, has about 30,000 former war refugees living primarily in Miami who were granted temporary visas during the Reagan administration which supported right-wing Contras in their efforts to oust the then ruling leftist Sandinista government. Their permits ran out last year, and Clinton must decide whether to invoke executive privilege and grant them legal status.

According to the U.S. Immigration and Naturalisation Service (INS), El Salvador and Guatemala are second and third behind Mexico among nations contributing illegal immigrants to the United States, with Honduras and Nicaragua also in the Top 10.
The INS puts the number of illegals from those four countries alone at 660,000, although estimates from Central American governments and human rights groups are much higher.

The money they and legal immigrants send back home is a leading source of foreign currency. El Salvador estimates 1.2 million of its people living in the United States sent home $1.086 billion in 1996, dwarfing the $339 million earned from its traditional top export, coffee.

"The numbers (of immigrants) are so great that we cannot ask President Clinton for something he cannot concede," Costa Rica's Solis said. "But we want to guarantee a dignified treatment. They (Clinton officials) have told us they are trying to make the law more flexible."
